profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional cancer center is conducting a design review of a proposed patient-reported outcomes workflow that will use the SF-36 in a survivorship registry. The proposal covers portal-based self-administration before follow-up visits, tablet completion in clinic, and telephone backup for patients who do not use the portal. The agenda is to review whether the current design preserves the intent of the SF-36 while fitting operational constraints, especially around timing of the first survey, mixed-mode administration, who counts as eligible, and whether the workflow is ready for a 6-week pilot. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the design for pilot with minor edits, or send it back for revision.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Psychometrics, patient-reported outcomes, longitudinal health-status measurement
members.background: Lena leads outcomes design for comparative-effectiveness studies at the cancer center and has previously published work using standardized health-status instruments in multisite registries.
members.private_state: She wants the workflow approved only if the resulting SF-36 data will still be defensible for benchmarking and future publications; she is especially wary of operational conveniences that quietly change what the instrument measures.
hidden_assumptions: A patient's 'baseline' SF-36 should mean the first assessment obtained before meaningful treatment exposure, not merely the first one captured in the system.
Telephone administration of the SF-36 means trained staff read the instrument verbatim and use only neutral repetition, without explanatory paraphrasing.
Calling the workflow 'comparable to published SF-36 use' implies the full 36-item instrument is completed as one administration occasion with standard wording and timing.
Because the SF-36 was designed for self-administration by people 14 years and older, adolescents in survivorship follow-up are naturally within scope unless someone explicitly excludes them.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Patient portal workflows, call-center operations, clinical program rollout
members.background: Ravi manages deployment of digital intake and follow-up tools across ambulatory programs and is responsible for fitting new instruments into existing portal, tablet, and telephone support processes.
members.private_state: He wants the design to pass review with minimal rework so the registry can launch on schedule using current staffing, portal automation, and contact-center scripts.
hidden_assumptions: A 'baseline' survey is simply the first completed SF-36 linked to enrollment, even if it happens after the first survivorship visit or initial therapy has already begun.
Telephone administration includes staff helping patients through the questionnaire in plain language so long as the response options map back to the official categories.
If the proposal still uses all 36 SF-36 items, splitting them across portal reminders or contact points is operationally the same instrument for pilot purposes.
When people say 'eligible patients,' they mean the adult registry population already supported by the portal and call-center consent workflow, not 14-17-year-olds.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the baseline SF-36
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to collecting a 'baseline' SF-36 before the pilot dashboard starts tracking change.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a pre-treatment or at least pre-meaningful-exposure assessment within the enrollment window, so later scores can be interpreted as change from an untreated starting point.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first completed assessment after registry onboarding, regardless of whether the patient has already had treatment or a survivorship visit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In registry design meetings, 'baseline' is a routine term that usually goes unexamined because both sides assume the first recorded measure is obviously the baseline; the divergence hides inside unstated assumptions about treatment timing.

misalignment_points.topic: What telephone administration allows staff to do
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to keep a 'telephone administration' option for patients who cannot use the portal.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes telephone administration means a standardized interviewer mode with verbatim item reading, fixed response categories, and no explanatory gloss beyond neutral repetition.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes telephone administration can include call-center staff translating items into simpler language, giving examples, and helping patients choose among response options as long as answers are entered into the official fields.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The SF-36 paper describes interviewer administration as legitimate, so both feel safe saying 'telephone administration' without specifying the interaction style; the operational details seem too mundane to spell out in a design review.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether a split completion still counts as the same SF-36 administration
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about using the 'same 36-item survey' across portal, tablet, and reminder workflows.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the 36 items are one administration occasion completed in one sitting or near-continuous session, preserving a single reference frame for scoring and interpretation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the survey is still the same SF-36 if 18 items are completed in the pre-visit portal check-in and the remaining 18 are finished through a reminder link or a follow-up call within a couple of days.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are indeed using the same item set and name, surface agreement feels genuine; neither expects the other to treat session boundaries as part of the instrument rather than just an implementation detail.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included when they say eligible patients
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to rolling the pilot out to 'all eligible survivorship patients' once the design is approved.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes eligibility includes adolescents aged 14-17, since the SF-36 can be self-administered by people 14 years and older and survivorship follow-up spans that age range.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes eligibility means adults already covered by the existing portal consent, call-center scripts, and registry operations, effectively 18 and older.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither sees age scope as a controversial design item because each assumes the operational boundary is already obvious from existing practice or from the instrument description; the phrase 'eligible patients' therefore passes without challenge.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure this is still defensible as SF-36 data, not just a convenient patient contact workflow. If they are using the same 36-item survey in the usual sense, completed as one administration occasion with standard wording, then I can support a pilot. What I do not want is a quiet redesign that makes future benchmarking impossible while everyone keeps calling it the SF-36.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Before we sign off on the survivorship pilot, I want to confirm the proposed SF-36 workflow is methodologically solid and still comparable to standard use. My main question is whether we're truly keeping the same 36-item survey across the workflow, even as we support different ways for patients to complete it.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to clear review without reopening the build. The design is straightforward: portal first, tablet if they arrive without having done it, telephone administration if they can't use digital tools, all within the adult registry operations we already run. If Lena hears that we are covering all eligible survivorship patients and not changing the item set, she should be comfortable enough to approve with minor edits.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's the design. We start with portal completion ahead of the follow-up visit, use tablet in clinic when needed, and keep a telephone administration option for patients who can't use the portal. That way we can reach all eligible survivorship patients before launch without creating a separate process by site.

turns.inner_thought: Good. The next issue is baseline timing. For change scores to mean anything, baseline has to be before meaningful treatment exposure, not just the first score that happens to land in the record. I assume they have aligned onboarding so the baseline SF-36 is captured early enough to serve as a real starting point.
turns.utterance: That helps. The other piece I want to check is timing. Will the baseline SF-36 be in place early enough that the dashboard can show meaningful change over time, rather than just giving us a first data point whenever the workflow happens to catch up?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, baseline is simply the first completed survey tied to registry enrollment. Usually that will come from portal check-in, and if outreach lands a bit later that's still fine because the first completed one becomes the baseline in the system. We do not have the staffing or enrollment logic to chase a stricter pre-exposure window, and I don't think we need it for a six-week pilot.
turns.utterance: Yes. For the pilot, baseline will be the first completed survey tied to enrollment, so the dashboard has a consistent starting point. In most cases that will come through the portal flow, and the system will anchor from there once the first one is in.

turns.inner_thought: If the first completed survey is obtained through the standard pre-visit flow, that should be acceptable. What I still need confidence about is session integrity. The same 36-item survey needs to function like one administration, not a patchwork assembled over multiple contacts. I'll ask about incomplete portal sessions without sounding obstructive.
turns.utterance: Okay. Since interpretation depends so much on keeping the same 36-item survey intact across modes, how is the portal flow handling patients who don't finish in one pass?

turns.inner_thought: This is the part I hope she won't see as a major issue. We split it operationally: the first half in pre-visit check-in, the rest by reminder link or follow-up call within a couple of days, but it's still the same 36 items and the same survey record in our system. From an implementation standpoint that's efficient and avoids losing completions.
turns.utterance: We've set it up so patients can continue if they don't complete it right away. The same 36-item survey follows them through the portal, and if needed we can finish it through a reminder workflow or during a follow-up contact, while still treating it as the same survey instance in the registry.

turns.inner_thought: As long as telephone administration means standardized interviewer administration, this could still be fine. The critical thing is that staff don't start interpreting items for patients or smoothing over confusing wording, because then we are no longer measuring the same construct. I should emphasize training and consistency.
turns.utterance: That makes sense operationally. The telephone administration path is useful, especially for patients who won't use the portal, but I'd want staff training to be very tight so the instrument stays consistent for patients who need that option.

turns.inner_thought: Training is already covered if we use the existing call-center approach. Our staff help people through forms in plain language all the time, and that's the only realistic way to keep calls from falling apart. As long as they land the patient in the official response fields, I consider that consistent enough for pilot use.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We can use the existing call-center script and training so staff know how to guide patients through telephone administration, keep them moving if wording slows them down, and help them get to the right response choice without dropping out of the call.

turns.inner_thought: If baseline and administration are handled appropriately, then my remaining concern is coverage. I need confidence that all eligible survivorship patients includes the adolescent follow-up population too, since the SF-36 is within scope for ages 14 and up and those patients are part of survivorship care here. I assume they're already accounted for unless someone says otherwise.
turns.utterance: Good. If those pieces are in place, what I mainly need is confidence that all eligible survivorship patients can complete it in the intended mode across follow-up, including the younger end of that group.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine within the adult registry population. Our current pilot covers the full eligible population already supported by the portal, consent, and call-center workflow; we can always extend later once the process is stable. I assume that's what she means by the younger end anyway—newer survivorship patients or younger adults, not minors outside the current operations.
turns.utterance: Yes, for the pilot we're covering the full eligible population that's already in the registry workflow, and that should give us broad enough reach to test the process end to end. Once we've proven it works, we can always expand from there.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds close. I still want the protocol language tightened so 'baseline' and administration consistency are clearly documented. If the write-up reflects standard expectations, I can approve the pilot and preserve the option for benchmarking and publications later.
turns.utterance: All right. It sounds close to ready from my side. I'd suggest a few documentation updates around baseline timing and administration consistency, but assuming those are reflected clearly, I don't see a reason to hold the pilot back.

turns.inner_thought: Great—that sounds like approval with minor edits, which keeps us on schedule. I'll revise the plan just enough to reflect the discussion, without changing the workflow design or launch date.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll circulate a revised pilot plan reflecting today's discussion and keep the launch date as is, so the team can move into build finalization and site readiness this week.
